## Conclusion: **YES**

Radiofrequency (RF) application in the posteroseptal region can alter retrograde atrial activation of a posteroseptal accessory pathway, even when the initial RF lesions do not successfully eliminate the pathway.

| Human study | Findings |
|---|---|
| **“Radiofrequency application to the posteroseptal region alters retrograde accessory pathway activation” (2000; PMID: 10729849)** | Electrophysiologic study of **3 patients** initially considered to have a single posteroseptal accessory pathway. Before RF, earliest retrograde atrial activation was at the **coronary sinus ostium**. After unsuccessful posteroseptal RF applications, the earliest activation shifted to the **right atrial free wall in 2 patients**. In the third, it shifted to the **distal coronary sinus**, mimicking a left free-wall pathway. Additional RF was required to eliminate the pathway/tachycardia. |
| **“Intraatrial conduction block in the right posteroseptal region after failed accessory pathway ablation” (2021; PMID: 34712560)** | Human right-posteroseptal case describing extensive RF near the tricuspid annulus after failed ablation. The report emphasizes that RF-related intra-atrial conduction disturbance can substantially alter atrial activation and complicate subsequent pathway localization, although the retrieved record provides fewer quantitative activation-sequence details. |

### Interpretation

The strongest direct evidence is the 3-patient electrophysiology series: posteroseptal RF changed the **earliest retrograde atrial activation site**, rather than merely abolishing conduction. The change was variable—toward the right atrial free wall in some patients and the distal coronary sinus in another—consistent with RF-induced intra-atrial conduction alteration or block that can obscure the original pathway pattern.

Therefore, the evidence supports:

**YES — RF application/ablation in the posteroseptal region can alter retrograde activation sequence and can confound assessment of residual accessory-pathway conduction.**

The evidence is compelling but limited in scale, consisting primarily of a small human series and case-level corroboration rather than a large controlled study.

Yes. In a human electrophysiology series of three patients with presumed single posteroseptal accessory pathways, initially unsuccessful RF applications shifted the earliest retrograde atrial activation from the coronary sinus ostium to the right atrial free wall in two patients and to the distal coronary sinus in one. Additional RF was needed to eliminate pathway conduction or tachycardia, indicating that the activation sequence could change before the pathway was eliminated. The evidence is limited by the small series and case-based corroboration.
